The suspected shooter at Bend, Oregon, Silver Rail Elementary School used a pump-action shotgun that his mother bought, according to the Associated Press (AP).

Breitbart News reported that the suspected shooter was 16 years of age, and CBS News pointed out that law enforcement indicated he was killed by a bystander.

Four innocents were killed in the incident. KATU 2 noted that “the victims were three children, ages 5, 8 and 11 and one teacher.”

There had been numerous reports during the late afternoon and evening that the attacker used a long gun. Now the AP explains that a law enforcement source confirmed it was a shotgun.

Law enforcement also observed that the attacker “forced his way into the school by shooting at locked doors.”

Actual Article Body:
By

Brittney Melton

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

A teenager opened fire at an elementary school in Bend, Ore., killing three children — ages 5, 8, and 11 — and a teacher, officials confirmed. A 7-year-old and a 54-year-old were hospitalized. A bystander killed the 16-year-old suspected shooter after following him into Silver Rail Elementary School, according to local officials. The suspected shooter has not been identified. Officials say he was a resident of Bend. He used a "long gun," which is similar to a rifle or shotgun, during the attack. His connection to the school — if any — remains unclear.

A candlelight memorial is seen out front of Silver Rail Elementary School on Oct. 15, 2026, in Bend, Oregon.
                
                    
                    Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

The Justice Department is suing California to stop the state from counting ballots that the government claims are from noncitizens. Three weeks before Election Day, the DOJ provided a flash drive containing the names of 20,000 people it suspected of being noncitizens on California's voter rolls to Los Angeles County's top voting official. The DOJ gave him 48 hours to investigate the names or face a lawsuit, which was filed yesterday.

Trump administration lawyers will argue today at a federal appeals court that White House papers belong to Trump rather than the American people. The case could end up in front of the conservative-leaning Supreme Court. The White House's claim comes after a series of actions during Trump's second term that challenged the limits put on the president after the Watergate scandal. For some 200 years, presidents could personally decide what to do with the papers they created in office. Then, Congress established the Presidential Records Act following disputes with Richard Nixon. Until this year, every president has followed this records law. Six months ago, the Trump administration moved to invalidate it. The move came after Trump was indicted on obstruction-of-justice charges for allegedly possessing classified documents at Mar-a-Lago, although a federal judge dismissed the case for technical reasons and the Justice Department later dropped it after Trump won reelection.

by Monika Evstatieva, senior producer on NPR's Investigations team

NPR's investigation finds that stores selling skincare products purchased from Mazal Group have routinely pressured shoppers, including older adults and people with disabilities, into buying expensive skincare products and services they did not want, could not afford or tried to refuse.
                
                    
                    Collage by Jackie Lay/NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

It all began with a tip. A colleague of mine had a friend in Ann Arbor who needed help. When I called her, she told me her elderly mom had been walking through a mall when a salesperson approached her with an eye cream sample. She went into a store called Beauty Essentials in Ann Arbor, Mich., and came out with $5,000 in skincare products she didn't want, tried to refuse, and couldn't return. But, she said, it wasn't an isolated incident. She posted on Facebook and connected with more than 30 people with complaints about the store. She asked me to look into it.

And so began an investigation that took place over more than a year. My reporting partner, Caley Fox Shannon, and I found similar complaints all over the country. We followed the trail, and found a network of mall skincare stores that systematically targeted older adults and people with disabilities across the United States. There was a link between them: one company, the California-based Mazal Group.

Over the past year, we spoke with more than 50 people, including customers who say they were taken advantage of, their family members and former employees. We looked at state and federal court lawsuits, hundreds of online reviews and nearly 500 consumer complaints we got through Freedom of Information Act requests. We went to stores selling products from Mazal Group in Virginia, Maryland and California, as well as the company's Chatsworth, Calif., headquarters.

You can read about what we found in NPR Investigations' whole report here, watch our documentary or listen on Consider This.

🎵 Music: Remi Wolf's new album, Mud, emerged from a period of significant personal change, including a breakup and becoming sober. Watch her talk about it and perform some songs on World Cafe.

🎮 Gaming: NPR's James Perkins Mastromarino got to play The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time early, ahead of its Nov. 5 release. He says, "The game's poised to ensnare old fans and entice new players."

Oregon elementary school teen gunman fired his mom’s shotgun at truck before rampage that left 3 kids, teacher dead: report

The Bend, Oregon, elementary school shooter who killed three students and a teacher used his mom’s shotgun to fire at a pickup truck before his crazed rampage, according to a report.

Actual Article Body:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

The Oregon teen who burst into an elementary school, killing three students and a teacher, used his mom’s shotgun to fire at a pickup truck before his deadly rampage, according to a report.

The unidentified 16-year-old shooter, a Bend resident, was heading towards Silver Rail Elementary School just before 1 p.m. Thursday when he was spotted by a man driving a red Toyota Tacoma pickup truck in the school’s parking lot, the Bend Source reported.

The boy was armed with a long gun, which a law enforcement source speaking on the condition of anonymity later told the Associated Press that the weapon was a pump-action shotgun his mom had bought.

The teen opened fire at the truck after the driver confronted him, shattering the rear window and leaving at least six large bullet holes in the car.

The boy then allegedly threw his weapon over a fence before jumping over onto the school’s property, while the man in the car called emergency dispatchers to report he had been “shot at multiple times by a person with a long gun.”

The shooter then picked his weapon up and fired several shots at the locks – breaking his way into the school, which serves children in kindergarten through fifth grade.

Cops arrived within three minutes of the first 911 call, but three kids, of the ages 5, 8 and 11, and a teacher were fatally shot. Another child, 7, and teacher, 54, were hospitalized in critical condition.

The boy was “shot by a community member who had seen [him] enter the school, pursued him into the school, and engaged him,” Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told reporters at a press conference Thursday.

Authorities didn’t say if the shooter had previously attended the school, if he knew his victims or if the heroic bystander who stopped the teen had a concealed weapons permit.

The shotgun was purchased by the boy’s mom, a law enforcement source briefed on the shooting said.

In Oregon, a person must be 18 to buy rifles and shotguns and 21 to purchase a handgun. Those under 18 can possess non-handgun weapons if they have parental consent. It’s unclear if the shooter had consent to use his mom’s weapon.

Bend La Pines school district previously banned all people, including those with concealed handling licences, from carrying firearms on district property, Oregon Public Broadcasting reported in 2022.

A separate provision of state law does allow lawfully possessed guns on school grounds if they are unloaded and locked in a vehicle, the outlet reported.

Krantz has warned the investigation into the shooting will be “long” and there has been an outpouring of grief among officials.

Rep. Janelle Bynum (D-Oregon) lamented, “our kids are getting shredded.”

“The most heartbreaking thing, as the details have surfaced, is that we have a child involved in the killing of other children,” she told CNN’s Anderson Cooper Thursday.“Multiple families are being impacted. This continues to happen.”

Meanwhile, former Bend Mayor Jeff Eager said, “You can’t imagine that it happens here.”

“Bend is a place that people move to from bigger cities,” he told CNN.

“They move here because it’s relatively safe here, they move here because we have schools you can walk your kids to.”

Tina Kotek, the Oregon governor, thanked the community member who “”heroically intervened to ⁠stop further loss of life” but said no one “should have to live through this kind of day.”

“And as we learn more about the children and the adults who have been killed or injured, and their families and their ​loved ones, we are going to do a lot of crying, and we are going to cry together, and we’re probably going to cry privately,” she said.

With Post wires
